proposal.title: BLM Revised Specified Requirements in the 2016 Waste Prevention Rule
proposal.description_short: BLM revised specified requirements in its 2016 Waste Prevention Rule for oil and gas operations.
proposal.description_medium: Interior announced on September 18, 2018, that BLM had finalized revisions to the 2016 Waste Prevention Rule. The Federal Register published the final rule on September 28, with an effective date of November 27. The rule rescinded specified requirements and revised other venting and flaring provisions; it did not rescind every part of the 2016 rule. These agency records document the rulemaking, not measured environmental outcomes.
proposal.description_long: On September 18, 2018, the Department of the Interior announced that the Bureau of Land Management had finalized a rule revising regulations from its 2016 Waste Prevention Rule. The Federal Register published the final rule on September 28, 2018; it took effect November 27. The rule identified specific requirements it rescinded, including those for waste-minimization plans, gas-capture percentages, well drilling and completion, pneumatic equipment, storage vessels, and leak detection and repair. It also revised provisions concerning venting and flaring and addressed when flaring associated gas from oil wells would be royalty-free under state or tribal regulation. The record supports a defined rule change rather than a claim that all 2016 standards were abolished. The Department’s press release and final rule are agency sources for the action and its stated rationale. They do not establish quantified methane reductions or other environmental consequences, so none are stated here.

proposal.title: Lyn Redwood Presented on Thimerosal at a June 2025 ACIP Meeting
proposal.description_short: NBC News reported that Lyn Redwood presented on thimerosal at the CDC advisory committee meeting on June 26, 2025.
proposal.description_medium: On June 26, 2025, Lyn Redwood presented on thimerosal at a meeting of the CDC’s Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices, NBC News reported. NBC identified Redwood as president emerita of Children’s Health Defense and described the presentation topic. This proposal reports the event; it does not state that the committee accepted her claims as policy.
proposal.description_long: On June 26, 2025, Lyn Redwood presented on thimerosal at a meeting of the CDC’s Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices, NBC News reported. NBC identified Redwood as a nurse practitioner and president emerita of Children’s Health Defense. The article described thimerosal as a mercury-based preservative formerly used in some vaccines and reported that Redwood’s presentation focused on it. NBC also reported that nearly all U.S. vaccines have contained no thimerosal or only trace amounts since 2001, with exceptions including some multidose flu-shot vials. After the presentation, the committee voted 5–1 to recommend single-dose thimerosal-free flu vaccines; one member abstained. That sequence does not show that Redwood’s remarks determined the vote, and the report does not establish that her claims were adopted as CDC policy. This account confines the claim to the reported presentation, its subject, and the subsequent committee vote. It makes no claim about a formal appointment or job title at CDC.

proposal.description_long: The Justice Department announced the Anti-Weaponization Fund on May 18, 2026, and described a $1.776 billion fund, a process for eligible claimants to seek compensation, and a five-member commission to review claims. Any account of individual award decisions, payout timing, or the underlying merits would require separate direct records or reporting.

proposal.description_long: A December 15, 2025 Cointelegraph article attributed to a New York Times investigation the finding that the Securities and Exchange Commission had “eased up on” about 60% of crypto enforcement cases under the Trump administration. Cointelegraph’s description includes different outcomes such as dismissals and pauses, so it does not support a headline stating that the SEC dropped more than 60% of cases. The linked New York Times article could not be accessed directly in this review, which means the underlying denominator, selection rules, and classification of each matter were not independently checked. The available evidence also does not establish that campaign contributions caused agency decisions, that every affected company had political ties, or that particular officials acted to provide a private benefit. The correction therefore attributes the percentage to Cointelegraph’s summary of the Times report and preserves the broader category “eased up on.” It does not turn that reported analysis into a verified count of dismissed cases or a finding of political favoritism. Case-specific conclusions would require the underlying investigation or docket-level review.
